findings.element: The horizon subtitle (.b-sub), the unfurl card title (.b-unfurlTitle), the print subtitle and the stepper ceiling refusal (.b-ceiling) — on any project actually created through owner-empty
findings.problem: The empty state asks when the day is and never asks what it is, and no control anywhere names it afterwards, so F.project.primaryDate.label stays the placeholder string "The day" and is then spent as a fact in four places. Driven: from owner-empty, typing 3 October 2026, pressing Set the day and adding one moment produces a horizon reading "79 / days / Saturday 3 October 2026 / The day"; pushing that moment to the ceiling prints "This is as far as it goes. The day is the last day.", which is not a sentence anyone wrote; and pressing Publish shows the card that lands in the couple's message titled "The day, Saturday 3 October 2026". The line that carries the whole feeling of the product — "Wedding day" in the fixture — is, on every plan a real owner starts, a placeholder, and it leaks into the one artifact that leaves the product. The empty state's own promise, "it is the only thing needed to start", is what creates this: true about starting, false about finishing.
findings.fix: Three changes. (a) In states["owner-empty"], after the date is accepted, ask the second question in the same slot rather than jumping straight to the plan: heading "What is the day?", label "The day is", placeholder "Wedding day", one button "Name it" and one "Skip for now" that goes on; write the answer to F.project.primaryDate.label. Change the hint that follows to "The day is set. Name it, then add moments." (b) Where label is empty, render no .b-sub at all, and build .b-unfurlTitle as the date alone rather than printing the placeholder and its comma. (c) Stop interpolating the label into the ceiling sentence — in setAway() and in the typed-date refusal use "This is as far as it goes. " + F.fmt.longYear(F.project.primaryDate.date) + " is the last day.", which reads "This is as far as it goes. Saturday 3 October 2026 is the last day." on every project, the fixture's included.

findings.element: owner-draft, its Publish control, and the publish screen it lands on (.b-pressTitle and the .b-live strap)
findings.problem: The new draft branch says "Only you can see this" and stamps "Updated 16 July 2026". Pressing its primary control, Publish, lands on a screen headed "Mara & Finn have had this since 15 July." and announces "The link is below." — the wording reserved for a plan somebody is already holding. Pressing "Back to the plan" then restores "Live since 15 July · anyone with the link can read it" and rolls the stamp back to "Updated 15 July 2026". In two clicks a plan nobody holds becomes a plan held since the day before it existed, and time runs backwards in the footer. The cause: states["owner-draft"] renders under a temporary draft record and restores the fixture's published record on the way out, so the draft half of the press heading — "Send it to Mara & Finn.", which the fresh-project path does reach and which reads correctly — never renders from the state built to show it. The gate asserts the publish VERB knows whether anyone is holding a copy; the screen that verb leads to does not.
findings.fix: In states["owner-draft"], set F.publication = { state: "draft", publishedAt: null } and F.updatedLabel to today, and do not restore them at the end of the builder. The existing transition in the copy handler (F.publication = { state: "published", publishedAt: F.today }) then does the flip once, where it belongs. Publish from the draft lands on "Send it to Mara & Finn." with "Ready to send. The link is below."; after Copy the link the same heading becomes "Mara & Finn have had this since 16 July.", the status line becomes "Live since 16 July · anyone with the link can read it", and the stamp stays at 16 July.

findings.problem: One cancellation is stated three times in three registers, and on the printed keepsake all three sit within 90px of each other: the title struck through, "Not going ahead" set under it, and "One of them did not happen." below that. The label is present tense and the sentence is past tense about the same moment. In the owner's disclosure the sentence swaps as you open it — closed it reads "2 done, the last of them 18 April. One thing is not going ahead.", open it reads "One of them did not happen." — one click, opposite tense, and a third noun ("thing", "them") where the product's noun everywhere else is "moment". Across the state matrix the same slot carries four grammars for one fact: the owner's count summary, the guest's named summary ("The Orchard reserved, 18 April. The city hotel shortlist is not going ahead."), the morning's verbless fragment ("Venue walk-through, 19 September.") and print's "One of them did not happen." That is the four-grammars-for-one-fact class the library already paid for, back in the block whose whole job is to state a fact the picture cannot.
findings.fix: One vocabulary for a cancelled moment — "not going ahead" — everywhere, and one shape for the closing sentence. Replace both dropped-note strings with the same partition in that vocabulary: dropped.length === 1 ? "One moment is not going ahead." : dropped.length + " moments are not going ahead.", so opening the disclosure changes the rows and nothing else. Then delete the owner-only count branch in the note builder and give all four surfaces the guest shape — last.title + ", " + F.fmt.medium(last.date) + "." followed by the dropped sentence — since the head already carries the total and does not need restating in prose.

findings.problem: One node reports every change, in four shapes: "Send the invitations moved 7 days later.", "Send the invitations is now hidden from guests.", "Send the invitations was removed.", "A moment was added." and "Renamed to Evening reception." The rename is the only entry that does not name the moment it changed — it names the value it changed to — so the single action whose undo restores a name is the single entry that never says whose name, or what it was. Four entries lead with the object, one leads with the verb, in a bar the owner reads dozens of times a day. Separately the moment's title is dropped into the machine's sentence undelimited, so the fixture's own imperative titles garden-path: "Send the invitations moved 7 days later." parses as an instruction before it parses as a report, and that is the string standing on the owner-undone frame.
findings.fix: One grammar, <moment> <what happened>, and the person's words set apart from the machine's. Change the rename entry to say: [from || "Untitled moment", " is now ", to || "Untitled moment", "."], matching the visibility entry it already resembles. In every entry wrap the leading name in h("span.b-undoName", { text: name }) instead of concatenating it into the text node, and add .b-undoName { font-weight: 600 } to b.css — weight 600 is on the ladder and is already what a person's words get in .b-title — so the title reads as the subject of the sentence rather than as its opening verb.

findings.problem: "Nothing is planned until 1 August." is the first full sentence under the horizon on every surface that is handed over — the phone, the desk pane and the printed keepsake — and it reports what the plan does not have. On the keepsake it sits directly above seven moments and a wedding day. For the owner it is a useful nudge about their own unfinished work; for the couple's families, opening this once on a phone and judging the company by that screen, the second thing the document says about the most important day of their life is that nothing is planned. Serving both audiences the same string with no branch is the right instinct — the wording is the half that was chosen for only one of them.
findings.fix: State the boundary rather than its absence, in one sentence for both audiences: build the note as "The first moment is on " + F.fmt.medium(first.date) + "." It names the same boundary the gate asserts, comes from the same single writer so it still follows a move, holds for owner and guest alike, and stops the handed-over document opening on a negative.

biggestWin: The document knows the difference between a thing that is true now and a thing that was true when it was sent, and it says so in plain words instead of hiding it. The card that lands in someone else's chat client reads "79 / days away when this was sent" — a cached preview that states its own expiry — and the same discipline runs through "Live since 15 July · anyone with the link can read it", through the print sheet's "79 days away on Thursday 16 July 2026", and through the ended screen, which names a state rather than a fault, gives the day, names Orla and closes with "Nothing has been deleted." The refusals are the best-written strings in the product: "That day has gone. Pick one still ahead." and "This is as near as it goes. Tomorrow is the soonest." are confident, unapologetic and human, with no hedging and no apology anywhere in the whole document. Sentence case is held everywhere, uppercase is reserved for section heads, there is not one exclamation mark, not one piece of jargon and not one word of product-speak in anything the audience reads. The empty state — "When is the day?" over a single field and one example — is the best single screen here and would not look out of place shipped by Linear.
